Meanwhile, 81% of all respondents feel pressure to be visible to demonstrate their commitment to work, while close to 70% were concerned that taking time away for parenting or caregiving could affect their career progression. 57% of respondents believe that they have experienced or observed caregiving-related career disadvantage, while only only 35% felt they could use flexible work arrangements without facing negative judgement or scrutiny.

Recognising changing career needs from its survey, ISCA is piloting FlexConnect, a flexible hiring initiative that connects experienced accountancy professionals seeking alternative work arrangements with businesses that need finance talent for specific periods or assignments.

The initiative offers employers access to professionals for contract, fractional and temporary roles, including support for project needs, peak workloads and employees taking extended leave.

Since the pilot began in September 2026, more than 100 accountancy professionals have registered their interest to explore flexible work opportunities, while receiving support from employers across industries, including public and private sector organisations, shares ISCA.

ISCA President Lee Boon Teck stresses that a strong profession “should offer more than one way” to build a successful career. He says: “As professionals move through different stages of life, their interests and priorities may change, but the experience and expertise they have developed remain valuable. At the same time, businesses need greater flexibility in how they access talent, whether to support a specific project, manage peak workloads or cover temporary staffing gaps.

“Through ISCA FlexConnect, we hope to bring these needs together and create more opportunities for professionals to remain engaged in the workforce. Our ambition is to make accountancy a profession where people can continue to grow and contribute throughout their careers.”

title: Lufthansa to eliminate 1,000 jobs at struggling flagship airline
article:
(Nov 20): Deutsche Lufthansa AG will cut 1,000 jobs at its namesake airline to turn around the unprofitable mainline unit, as high fuel costs put more pressure on Europe’s largest aviation group.

The company will reduce full-time positions at hubs in Munich and Frankfurt, according to a letter by management to employees seen by Bloomberg. Lufthansa Airlines also plans to further reduce capacity on short- and medium-haul routes and shrink its fleet of Airbus A320 aircraft, switching to the smaller A220 type, it said.

The planned reductions are the second culling in little over a year and reveal the extent of the struggles to revive the fortunes of the airline’s flagship product. The airline group announced last September that it intended to cut 4,000 administrative jobs by 2030.

Lufthansa is undergoing its biggest efficiency drive in years as high jet-fuel prices and an underperforming mainline airline weigh on results. Lufthansa Airlines posted an operating loss of €180 million ($232 million) in the first nine months.

“After two years of the turnaround, we have to acknowledge that the original measures are no longer sufficient to secure our future,” management wrote in the letter. “In fact, 2026 has set us back: the war in the Middle East, persistently high fuel costs, nine days of strikes and our already very high cost base have made the situation more acute.”

Lufthansa’s new supervisory board chairman, Johannes Teyssen, said earlier this year that “significantly greater efforts” may be needed to improve the airline’s flagging performance after losing ground to rivals in what he called self-inflicted damage.

See also: US flight chaos persists with thousands of cancellations, delays

The measures revealed on Friday come as Lufthansa tries to resolve a dispute with labour unions, though no agreement had been reached so far.

title: CDL, DBS, SingPost, subsidiaries of listed companies, to recognise Green 100 Bronze credential for procurement
article:
A group of nine companies and the government will be recognising a new Green 100 Bronze credential as a qualifying credential in their procurement frameworks, according to an announcement on Nov 20. The Bronze credential builds on the Green 100 Essential badge launched earlier during the year.

These nine companies, or “queen bees”, include Mainboard-listed City Developments Limited (CDL), DBS and Singapore Post (Singpost), as well as Genting Singapore’s Resorts World Sentosa, Capitaland Investment’s The Ascott Limited and CDL’s Millennium Hotels & Resorts. Cushman & Wakefield, Mandai Wildlife Group and SMRT Corporation round up the group.

Through tapping suppliers with the Green 100 Bronze credential, large companies could potentially have a way to monitor, report and reduce emissions across their value chains.

In addition, the government will recognise Green 100 badges (starting from Bronze) as an additional, alternative pathway for firms to meet existing government procurement sustainability requirements. This will be done progressively and will start with large construction services tenders above $50 million and ICT hardware tenders above $10 million.

Currently, sustainability-related considerations are assigned 5% of evaluation points for such tenders. Full implementation details will be released to suppliers in due course, the announcement shared.

These Green 100 developments will “open doors” for SMEs, says climate action ambassador Ravi Menon, who is co-chair of Council for a Competitive Climate Transition (C3T). Singapore Business Federation (SBF) CEO Kok Ping Soon is the other co-chair.

See also: OCBC sustainability chief says ESG saw pushback on how it was pursued; eyes ‘sexy’ tech for net-zero

“SMEs’ emissions are the Scope 3 emissions of the larger companies subject to climate reporting,” remarks Menon, who made the afore-mentioned announcements at the Singapore Fintech Festival (SFF). The SFF is organised by the Global Finance & Technology Network (GFTN), which is chaired by Menon.

From FY2026 onwards, constituents of the STI must report Scope 3 greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. To do so effectively, these large companies will need emission information from companies across their value chains, adds Menon.

Launched in May by C3T, Green 100 is a national initiative that brings together large enterprises who will each mobilise 100 SMEs within their supply chains and business networks to start sustainability reporting and capability-building. The initiative is aligned with Technical Reference 149:2026 (TR 149:2026), a framework launched by the Singapore Standards Council (SSC) to help organisations assess their environmental sustainability performance and identify areas for improvement.

See also: Singapore wants to mobilise US$500 mil investment to build agri-food resilience

To date, 33 queen bees have joined the movement and more than 280 businesses have received the Green 100 Essential badge on the Green 100 platform. The Green 100 Bronze credential is introduced as a step up from the Green 100 Essential badge, and incentivises businesses to augment their sustainability efforts beyond reporting.

Green 100 helps SMEs progress from measuring their environmental footprint to taking practical steps to improve their sustainability performance. While Essential focuses on tracking baseline metrics such as energy, water, fuel consumption and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, Bronze requires SMEs to set environment targets and put in place policies and actions to manage their resource use and emissions, as well as extends tracking to include waste management.

SMEs seeking to obtain Green 100 Bronze must undergo independent assessments by accredited conformity assessment bodies (CABs) to verify that their reported environmental data meets the Bronze requirements of TR 149:2026. These assurance statements are based on a 12-month reporting period and are subject to annual reverification.

“Many SMEs lack the resources and expertise to measure their carbon footprints, let alone take measures to reduce them,” says Menon. “We must make it easier for SMEs to go green, and more rewarding for them to do so.”

RWS assistant vice president of procurement Andy Teo highlights that Green 100 aligns with RWS’s sustainability goals., which include mitigating Scope 3 emissions. He adds that Green 100 was unique and “very relatable” for SMEs due to its accessibility.

Menon, who is the former managing director of the Monetary Authority of Singapore, adds that international carbon pricing mechanisms, such as the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, require SMEs supplying exporters into these markets will also have to measure their carbon footprints or otherwise risk being cut off from the exporters’ supply chains.

To Menon, measurement is only the beginning and sustainability will scale only if it pays off. “Few SMEs will invest in sustainability simply because they are told to do so; many will if it helps them to win a contract or lower their financing costs,” he reasons. “Procurement and financing are where sustainability turns into money.”

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

DBS chief sustainability officer Kelvin Wong believes that Green 100 gives SMEs a strong business case to build their sustainability capabilities. “By recognising these efforts in our procurement processes, we can encourage more businesses to take action and build more resilient supply chains,” says Wong.

Meanwhile, the Singapore government’s chief sustainability officer, Lim Tuang Liang, says that due to the differing green procurement standards practiced by government agencies, SMEs faced an “onslaught” of procurement compliance process. According to Lim, approximately 6% of GDP can be tied back to green criteria of government procurement.

“So we wanted to look at how we can actually think about harmonising some of these procurement standards, offering it to companies and organisations … so that then we can collectively reduce the compliance costs for companies,” he explains.

To reduce the time needed by SMEs to attain Bronze, the Green 100 platform will integrate sustainability disclosure preparation and independent verification by third-party CABs into a single user journey. This service is available now.

The platform will help SMEs automatically retrieve their utilities data from Corppass and uploaded invoices, and will avail AI tools to help businesses develop sustainability strategies, policies and targets to strengthen sustainability readiness in line with TR149:2026. SMEs will also be able to submit their completed information directly to a panel of accredited Green 100 CABs directly through the platform for independent assessment.

Furthermore, the Government will provide grant support to help eligible companies cover training, consultancy and first-time assessment costs. Further details will be made available in due course.

Beyond digital capabilities, SBF and Gprnt, the technology provider for Green 100, will work with Green 100 ecosystem partners to provide onboarding workshops, training programmes, and other capability-building initiatives to support SMEs at different stages of their sustainability journeys.

Menon also presented a future for Green 100, which aims to broaden participation in Green 100 and deepen the recognition of sustainability credentials. To this end, C3T will convene public-private dialogues next year, to explore how Green 100 can be progressively expanded and recognised across more companies and organisations.

It will also engage more queen bees and SMEs, and create more Green 100 “value unlocks” in sustainable financing and sustainable procurement.

Menon also envisions Green 100 expanding beyond local shores. As national sustainability initiatives develop, we can explore mutual recognition across them,” he says. “Over time, an SME could demonstrate its credentials across borders, opening up new opportunities in regional supply chains, trade, and financing.”

One SME who has joined Green 100 and is taking steps to become more sustainable is Orapi Maintenance Asia, a manufacturer and supplier of professional hygiene, cleaning, and industrial maintenance chemical consumables across Asia.

According to Orapi CEO Pierre Buillas, joining Green 100 was a “natural step” for the company. “We already had several sustainability initiatives in place, but we wanted to bring more structure to our approach and better measure our progress,” he shares.

Through the Green 100 platform, Orapi and other SMEs found a fast and convenient way to input information and obtain their Scope 1 and 2 emissions, improving transparency and preparing for future requirements. “The programme provides a practical framework for SMEs like us to understand and report their environmental performance,” adds Buillas.

To become more sustainable, the company has installed on the roof of its premises nearly 650 solar photovoltaic panels that can generate up to 400KWp of electricity. Not only has the company reduced its carbon footprint from energy use, Orapi enjoys a net annual financial benefit of around $25,000 with the solar panels, with the firm using 15% of the energy generated and selling 85% to the grid.

“Sustainability does not necessarily require large investment,” says Buillas. “For example, the solar installation I mentioned previously was implemented with almost no upfront investments, thanks to an energy buyback arrangement.”

Orapi has also electrified its fleet, replacing its diesel-fueled vehicles with electric-powered ones, saving around $10,000 annually for the company.

On the business front, Orapi reports that it is seeing more sustainability criteria and requests for sustainability information in tenders. While he says it is still too early to link the company’s sustainability initiatives to contract wins, he says that sustainability enables the company to participate in the tenders with sustainable prerequisites.

However, some customers have misconceptions about sustainability, believing that it comes with costs that exceed corresponding benefits. To change these belief, Orapi works closely with customers, sharing its experience and the value of sustainability in helping companies enter more profitable markets.

“Our objective is not to follow the trend, but to anticipate customer expectation, and also market expectation in terms of sustainability,” says Buillas. “It's a way for us to differentiate ourselves and to bring something of value to the market and to the customer through sustainability.”

title: UK is the ‘best house in a bad neighbourhood,’ UBS Wealth says
article:
(Nov 20): UBS Global Wealth Management is betting on gains for the pound and UK gilts, confident that Britain’s political stability and efforts to curb spending will give it an edge over much of the euro area.

Sterling is UBS Wealth’s preferred Group-of-10 currency, due to its yield advantage over the euro, Swiss franc and Japanese yen. It also favors short- to medium-dated UK government bonds on a view the Bank of England will raise interest rates less aggressively than expected.

For many investors, those factors set the UK apart from the euro area, where large budget deficits and political discord ahead of elections are clouding the outlook. Debt-laden France is seen as a particular risk, increasingly leading traders to shun the euro.

“What we have learned for 2027 is the UK could be the best house in a bad neighbourhood,” said Dean Turner, an economist and macro strategist in UBS Wealth’s chief investment office.

In Europe, the “base case” is for election-linked volatility, he added.

See also: Thailand says US agrees to lower forced-labour tariff to 10%

Many investors have warmed to British assets since Prime Minister Andy Burnham took office at the end of July. Interest has picked up further after the government unveiled a budget that avoided big spending increases and pushed to boost ties with the European Union.

Britain’s relatively high yield gives the pound an advantage against most other developed-market currencies, UBS Wealth said in its year-ahead report. Resilient economic activity, a 4% interest rate and the prospect of further policy tightening should keep sterling’s carry advantage intact, the report said.

“Wide rate differentials and contained currency volatility should support total returns, particularly against lower-yielding currencies,” it added.

See also: Australia’s jobless jump prompts traders to price rate cuts

On gilts, UBS Wealth’s bullishness rests partly on the view that markets are pricing more tightening from the BOE than is likely to materialise. While money markets expect at least three interest-rate hikes by end-2027, Turner sees just one more — in February — as the most likely outcome.

That would leave room for the two-year yield to fall to about 4.5% by December 2027, according to Turner, from current levels around 4.96%.

For gilts, “the risks here still look pretty favourable,” Turner said. “The fiscal consolidation story and the UK stand out.”

title: SpaceX sold US$32 bil of AI chip debt at yields topping 8% — Bloomberg
article:
(Nov 20): SpaceX sold US$32 billion ($41 billion) of bonds to fund its purchase of artificial intelligence (AI) chips on Thursday, in a complicated and relatively high-yielding transaction that may serve as a model for a wave of similar financings to come.

The debt offering was designed to keep the borrowing off SpaceX’s balance sheet, and is part of a more than US$40 billion financing that also includes bank loans. The deal will effectively allow SpaceX to buy Nvidia Corp chips that the rocket, satellite and AI company will lease for about five years.

The debt was sold on Thursday in three parts, according to people with knowledge of the matter. Goldman Sachs Group Inc and Apollo Global Management Inc ran the transaction, the people said, asking not to be identified as they are not authorised to speak publicly. Representatives of the firms and SpaceX didn’t respond to requests for comments.

The biggest of the three portions sold on Thursday, about US$25.2 billion of Class A3 notes, were priced at a yield of 8.259%, a relatively high level for an investment grade security. The average US high-grade note yielded 5.95% on Thursday, according to Bloomberg index data. The bonds also offered a premium over SpaceX’s existing debt from its June offering, which tanked in the secondary market after the securities started trading.

Investors had already committed to buy about US$26 billion of the bonds earlier, with the final US$6 billion, part of the Class A3, offered on Thursday. Many of the securities were sold to investors that focus on blue-chip corporate bonds.

The chips will be bought through a special-purpose vehicle known as Saturn Funding Trust and managed by an Apollo-backed entity. SpaceX is leasing from the vehicle, and has committed to make the payments even if the equipment fails or there’s an extraordinary occurrence like a natural disaster, known as a “force majeure” event.

See also: Investors warn bond rout not over after week of soaring yields

The financing structure is expected to help SpaceX maintain investment-grade credit ratings — a critical competitive advantage for many of the biggest companies competing in the AI space, because it allows them to borrow more money, faster.

Bret Johnsen, SpaceX’s chief financial officer, highlighted the company’s “strong investment-grade balance sheet” on a conference call with investors after posting results last month. SpaceX sold US$86.2 billion of stock in a June initial public offering and priced US$25 billion of high-grade corporate bonds days later.

Companies will need some US$1.5 trillion to pay for computer chips driving the AI build-out, and deals to finance these purchases will probably become more commonplace, Scott Goodwin, a co-founder of hedge fund manager Diameter Capital Partners, said at a conference this week.

See also: South Korea fines bond dealers record US$1.2 bil over collusion

Tech companies are tapping all corners of capital markets to raise the trillions of dollars needed for data centres and other AI infrastructure, testing the depths of investor demand and risking indigestion. Thursday’s debt sale came one day after AI giant Anthropic PBC completed the largest-ever initial public offering (IPO), exceeding SpaceX’s own IPO.

After investors lost money on SpaceX’s earlier unsecured bond offering, “we have definitely had concern from clients that are very sceptical about how is this deal going to go”, said Davis Hebert, the head of technology, media and telecom at research firm CreditSights. “I do think that’s why the pricing on this is really wide to try and attract participation for more traditional investors.”

The latest deal structure was complex for investment-grade investors to analyse, particularly as financing deals tied to AI graphics processing units, or GPUs, are relatively new, with investors still assessing risks related to the lifecycle and valuation of the chips.

BlackRock Inc, Goldman Sachs Asset Management and KKR & Co accounts were among the anchor investors in the latest transaction, the company said in October.

SpaceX is raising a total of more than US$40 billion through the broader transaction, which includes the bonds priced on Thursday and a senior secured loan. The debt package will be used to pay for about US$47.3 billion of GPU equipment, namely Nvidia’s latest Rubin chips, earlier documents showed. Delivery of the chips is expected to begin in January.

title: Taiwan’s stock benchmark plunges 18% in worst week since 1991
article:
(Nov 20): Taiwan’s tech-heavy stock market witnessed another sell-off on Friday as the global artificial intelligence (AI) trade came under further strain, sending the island’s benchmark to its worst week since 1991.

The Taiex Index tumbled 6.2%, taking its losses for the week to almost 18%. That’s even as local authorities stepped in to stabilise the market by tightening curbs on short selling twice this month.

Tech stocks across Asia slumped on Friday as Anthropic PBC’s blockbuster listing failed to ease broader doubts over the AI trade, with investors unsure whether returns will justify the vast sums being spent and borrowed to fund the technological buildout. Shares of Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, fell 4.7% in after-hours US trading. Tech makes up more than 70% of the Taiex, leaving it particularly susceptible to swings in sentiment towards the sector.

“The listing of Anthropic failing to lift the market sentiment is the main hit on AI across Asia,” said Steven Leung, executive director at UOB Kay Hian Hong Kong Ltd. In Taiwan, further declines in share prices are intensifying the pressure from margin calls, triggering forced deleveraging, he added.

Taiwan’s Financial Supervisory Commission on Thursday tightened curbs on short selling to help stabilise the local equity market. Effective Friday, the commission will cap the volume of intraday short-sale orders for borrowed securities at 1% of a stock’s average daily trading volume over the prior 30 days, down further from the 3% limit set earlier this month. Certain hedging and market-making activities will be exempt, the FSC said in a statement.

See also: Japan Tobacco hit by US$8.9 bil charge on Russia seizure

Aggregate short interest as a percentage of float across Taiwanese listed equities stood at 5.28% as of Thursday, just a little lower than around 5.49% on Nov 6, the day when local authorities first restricted short-selling activities, according to S3 Partners, a data analytics firm.

“Limiting short-selling activity does not eliminate underlying bearish sentiment or selling pressure from investors reducing existing long exposure,” said Matthew Unterman, head of research at S3 Partners. “Hedge funds maintaining established bearish positions may have limited incentive to cover solely because new short-selling activity has become more restrictive, particularly if their underlying investment thesis remains intact.”

The AI trade, a key force behind this year’s global equities rally, is facing multiple headwinds. In recent days, tech outages and leadership turmoil at Nvidia Corp have cast a pall over the sector’s outlook, adding to existing concerns about stretched valuations, uncertain returns on massive AI investments and the prospect of greater industry scrutiny following the Democrats’ sweep of Congress in the US midterms.

See also: Taiwan tightens short selling curbs to help support stock market

Forced selling by retail investors was the main driver of Taiwan’s worst stock selloff in four months that took place on Monday, a trend that may extend and pressure the market further, according to Barclays plc note earlier this week.

“The AI concerns, including the latest development with Nvidia, have been weighing on Taiwanese stocks particularly hard,” said Xin-Yao Ng, a fund manager at Aberdeen. “At this point, margin loan balance is still too high in Taiwan and that needs to come down more.”

The Taiex has now lost more than a quarter of its value since hitting a record high on Oct 6, paring its year-to-date gain to about 24%. Foreign outflows have added to the pressure, with global funds having sold more than US$56 billion ($72 billion) of local stocks on a net basis so far this quarter.

“Every day it seems like the day to bottom fish as technicals suggest better risk-reward level here,” Goldman Sachs Group Inc’s sales desk wrote in a commentary to institutional clients on Friday. “But if anything learned from 2026 momentum, that is the highs can go higher, so now the lows may go lower.”

title: DayOne said to pause US IPO plans on data center, market concerns — Bloomberg
article:
(Nov 20): DayOne Data Centers Ltd has put plans for its multibillion-dollar US initial public offering on hold, people familiar with the matter said, as investors question the sustainability of frothy valuations for digital infrastructure supporting the artificial intelligence boom.

The data center operator, whose biggest customer is ByteDance Ltd, the Chinese owner of TikTok, was initially intending to raise as much as US$5 billion from an IPO as soon as the fourth quarter, Bloomberg News reported previously. But it started to reassess options including a delay or a smaller listing as volatility increased around data centers and AI stocks.

Singapore-based DayOne may still pursue an IPO in 2027 if the situation and market sentiment improve, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information isn’t public. The company filed for the IPO in October and has been working with Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan Chase & Co, Bank of America Corp, Citigroup Inc and BNP Paribas SA on the listing.

Deliberations are ongoing and no final decisions on the IPO have been made, the people said. A representative for DayOne declined to comment.

Doubts about the potential payoff from massive investments into AI have fuelled volatility in global markets. The Nasdaq 100 has dropped more than 6% this month, heading for its worst November performance since 2008. Still, Anthropic PBC staged a record-breaking US$107.3 billion IPO and private placement and rose 17% on its trading debut on Thursday, becoming the world’s seventh-most valuable company.

Other data center-related companies have either pulled or delayed their IPO plans amid investor concerns in the sector. Last month, Firmus Grid Ltd abandoned its attempt at one of Australia’s biggest-ever initial public offerings, while Blackstone Inc-backed AirTrunk is delaying a listing of a real estate investment trust in Singapore until next year.

See also: The biggest winners in Anthropic’s landmark IPO

DayOne has hyperscale facilities in countries including Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia, which have seen a boom in data center development, fuelled by demand from Chinese tech companies like ByteDance and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd.

The US this week put interim rules on those four countries to restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips and servers, telling data center operators they’ll need a licence to purchase American tech hardware.

title: Nordic Group secures approximately $58.3 million worth of new contracts
article:
Nordic Group announced it has secured new contracts of around $58.3 million, of which $44.9 million worth of new contracts comes from its engineering solutions group, while the remaining $13.4 million from the engineering services group.

The group adds that the new contracts come from a range of sectors, which includes marine & offshore, semiconductor, defence, petrochemical and more. These contracts were awarded from new and repeat customers.

For the semiconductor sector, Nordic was awarded with the maiden process exhaust system contract in Gujarat, India, while the remaining are adhoc projects, maintenance, tool install, and hook-up services and machining and assembly work.

“These contracts are valued at around $24 million and will mainly be completed from 4QFY2026 to 4QFY2027,” the group says.

For the marine & offshore sector, the new contracts which are worth $18.7 million comprises mainly for the manufacture of valves and actuators, control and tank gauging systems. The contract covers 90 vessels, with deliveries scheduled from 4QFY2026 to 2QFY2030.

For the petrochemical sector, the new contracts are valued at $13.4 million and are mainly maintenance contracts for scaffolding and insulation work, with contract duration ranging between one to five years, which ends between FY2026 and FY2030.

See also: Lincotrade secures $81.1 mil in new contracts in 1QFY2027, order book hits $149.5 mil

Nordic Group expects the latest contract win to have no material impact on its consolidated net tangible assets per share and earnings per share for the current financial year.

Shares of Nordic were unchanged at 48 cents during the midday break.

title: Nextdc says it will no longer develop data centres near homes
article:
(Nov 20): Australian data centre company Nextdc has vowed not to develop sites near residential areas after community opposition and power constraints delayed a major expansion project.

The company last month said its M3 expansion in Melbourne had been delayed after community protests prompted power company Jemena to pause the installation of power poles. The news sparked Nextdc’s biggest single-day share price slump on record.

“There’s growing opposition to data centres in Australia and worldwide,” outgoing chairman Douglas Flynn said at the company’s annual meeting Friday in Sydney. “We do not intend to pursue new development opportunities that are near residential properties.”

The fallout from the M3 problems has deepened shareholder tensions. Some 72% of votes were cast against the company’s remuneration plan — the second straight year investors have largely rejected the company’s pay plan. Still, shareholders voted against spilling the board, a ballot triggered when more than 25% of votes oppose the remuneration report for two consecutive years.

Shares fell as much as 5.5% in Sydney trading on Friday, even as the company gave a slight upgrade to its revenue and earnings guidance.

See also: Thailand sees new US chip curbs as risk to data centre drive

“Would we buy this site again tomorrow? No we wouldn’t,” said Flynn, referring to M3, adding that the final development wouldn’t be “as ugly” as the original industrial site that had long been there. He said the board was working closely with Jemena regarding M3 and a path forward.

Nextdc has paused new commitments and plans to only commit new capital selectively, focusing on projects with customer contracts, expected returns above its cost of capital, sufficiently advanced power and planning, as well as funding in place.

Following the M3 delay, chief executive officer Craig Scroggie last month gave up his short-term and long-term bonuses for the 2027 financial year, while the company’s non-executive directors agreed to a 10% reduction in their fees.

See also: GIC, Saudi Telecom bid for UK’s Pure Data Centres stake — Bloomberg

The board also withdrew a resolution to seek shareholder approval to boost the maximum annual remuneration of non-executive directors to A$2.5 million (RM6.85 million) from A$2.2 million.

Asked on Friday about potential strategy changes at Nvidia Corp following founder Jensen Huang’s departure, Scroggie said he had a “high degree of confidence” the company would continue supporting key neocloud customers, which make up part of Nextdc’s client base.

Nvidia, the world’s largest chipmaker, in September named Nextdc as one of eight infrastructure partners it was collaborating with to deliver up to a two-gigawatt AI factory buildout in Australia by 2027.

Earlier this month, Goodman Group and Digital Realty Trust Inc jointly bought a 9.9% stake in the company, opening the door to potential collaboration.

title: Gold set for worst week since March on hawkish Fed, AI sell-off
article:
(Nov 20): Gold fell for a fifth day — heading for the biggest weekly decline since March — as a hawkish US Federal Reserve (Fed) signalled more interest-rate hikes and a rout in artificial intelligence (AI) stocks pushed investors to sell the metal to cover losses.

Bullion tumbled as much as 2.4% to below US$3,540 an ounce on Friday, on track to lose nearly 9% in a week that’s seen the metal slide to the lowest since September 2025. Silver has fallen about 14% in the same period. Fed Bank of Chicago president Austan Goolsbee on Thursday joined a number of central bank officials who have hinted at interest-rate hikes, saying he would consider all options to counter stubborn US inflation.

The prospect of tighter monetary policy kept Treasury yields elevated, with 10-year borrowing costs poised to match a 2007 run of 29 closes above 5% in the same year. Globally, investors are betting that major central banks, including the Fed, European Central Bank and Bank of England, will keep rates largely unchanged for years once they’ve finished hiking at the end of 2027.

Higher interest rates and yields are typically negative for gold, which doesn’t pay interest. A gauge of the dollar has also risen 0.7% this week, making bullion priced in the US currency more expensive for most buyers.

Gold is “now firmly in an air pocket, with very little technical support until the US$3,300 and US$3,400 region”, said Justin Lin, a strategist at Global X ETFs. The metal “looks very fragile now, and I struggle to see what could turn momentum around just yet”, he said.

See also: Gold slumps below US$3,800 as Fed officials signal more rate hikes

Bullion has fallen by about a third since the US-Iran war began in late February, as higher energy costs fueled inflation. The precious metal has also been caught up in a rout in technology stocks, with global equities set for their longest losing streak in more than three years driven by concerns around the AI trade.

Spot gold fell 2.3% to US$3,543.19 an ounce at 10.15am in Singapore. Silver dropped 2.3% to US$41.98 an ounce, after sinking nearly 5% in the previous session. Platinum and palladium also declined.

title: Xi, Trump, Putin agree to increase supply of global fuels
article:
(Nov 20): The leaders of the US, China and Russia agreed to boost the supply of fuels in a world that’s seen prices surge as a result of wars being waged by two of the three military superpowers.

President Xi Jinping hosted what he called a “groundbreaking” discussion with Presidents Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin on Thursday in Shenzhen, China. The discussion spanned issues from Ukraine and denuclearisation to the management of major-power disputes.

The unprecedented trilateral meeting had alarmed world capitals and raised concerns about carving up spheres of influence by the three military giants. For their part, the trio agreed in a joint statement to reform the United Nations, curtail the International Criminal Court (ICC) and avoid nuclear war.

They also “plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations” and reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows. The statement didn’t spell out what that would entail.

In theory, the pledge could offer some relief to stressed global fuel markets, where supplies have tightened and prices for products like diesel have surged due to disruptions caused by the wars in Ukraine and Iran. The three nations are oil-refining giants.

In practice, though, Russia’s processing capacity has been hobbled by drone strikes on its plants, US fuelmakers are already going flat out, while China’s imports of crude oil, which are integral to churning out refined products, have been stymied during much of the Middle East conflict.

See also: Oil set for third weekly drop as ample supply outweighs war risk

Xi warned at the start of the meeting that major-power rivalry breeds global instability and called for regular exchanges between China, Russia and the US. The meeting, held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, lasted roughly an hour and a half.

At the start of the gathering, Trump said, “We are really making history.” He added that the three have a special responsibility to maintain open dialogue, and said they would discuss issues including nuclear weapons and the Ukraine war.

See also: Vietnam triples LNG imports as El Niño saps hydropower output

“No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech,” Trump said. “Together, we are choosing a different course.”

Putin highlighted that the trio all represent victorious nations of World War II, and bear the task of preserving and strengthening the system of international law established at that time. The International Criminal Court issued an arrest order for Russia’s leader in 2023.

The Russian president said the group should also should discuss food and energy security. Costs of both agriculture and energy products have soared in recent years thanks to the disruptions in trade caused by the war in Ukraine and Trump’s February 2026 attacks on Iran.

The impact of the three-way agreement to boost refined products at one level is meaningful, given that it comes from two of the world’s largest oil producers — the US and Russia — and the world’s biggest crude importer: China. But what exactly the three can do isn’t immediately clear.

In the US, crude oil processing rates are already the highest for the time of year in three decades. For its part, China issues quotas on its fuelmakers, telling them what fuels they are allowed to export. Meanwhile Russia would need Ukraine to stop attacking its refineries if it were to boost supplies for a sustained period.

Moscow also remains under sweeping oil-related sanctions from the US, Europe and UK in response to its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, though the US recently issued waivers to those restrictions in a bid to boost the amount of fuel available on global markets. Shipments of Russian diesel have struggled to find willing buyers and there was bipartisan blowback on the easing of restrictions from both Republicans and Democrats.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Much of the world has been sceptical about the idea of the heads of the three nations being able to reduce international risks. Concerns about the optics of the meeting were all the more acute in western capitals, where Putin is widely regarded as a pariah due to Russia’s war on Ukraine, and many object to his being feted on such a global stage.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that US negotiators will debrief allies meeting in Berlin on the outcome of the talks in China.

Trump, who regularly refers to his warm personal relations with foreign leaders as driving policy outcomes, shrugged off any such concerns earlier on Thursday, telling Fox News that he was meeting with Xi and Putin at the same time “because they work together, have a relationship”. He referred to the warm greeting he received from Xi on Wednesday, describing their relationship as “great”, and later called Putin “my friend”.

“It’s an honour to be with Vladimir,” Trump said at the start of the trilateral.

Both Xi and Trump raised the issue of reducing nuclear risks, though Putin avoided the topic in his remarks. The Kremlin has been resorting to nuclear saber-rattling recently among setbacks on the battlefield in Ukraine.

China’s official Xinhua News Agency said the host leader’s talking points in the meeting included a call for establishing a world free of nuclear weapons.

Trump said of such weapons that “it’s very hard to give them up as a leader of a country”. Even so, the three leaders are “uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth, and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used”, he said.

The US and Russia together have some 86% of the world’s nuclear weapons, with China a distant third but its numbers rising, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, SIPRI. That’s left Beijing with little incentive to engage in reduction.

Xi’s talking points included a recommendation that the three countries maintain regular high-level exchanges, and ensure smooth dialogue channels at all levels. The three nations should act cautiously and avoid crossing the other sides’ red lines. In his opening remarks, Xi called the gathering “of groundbreaking significance”.

The inclusion of language on the ICC in the joint statement follows regular blasts of that body by the Trump administration. The ICC, of which the US isn’t a member, has issued an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, a long-time Trump ally, based on his war in Gaza.

While the trilateral encounter has drawn parallels with Yalta in 1945, when the heads of the three dominant military powers of the day — the US, UK and Soviet Union — met to discuss the end of World War II and the post-war future, expectations of concrete results have been low.

Today’s Russia is very much the junior partner, with an economy less than one-seventh China’s size and an even smaller fraction of America’s.

Nevertheless, Putin appeared emboldened by his inclusion in the various meetings in Shenzhen. He used a speech to APEC business leaders on Wednesday to rail against “failed attempts” to isolate Russia and claiming that his nation was emerging stronger.

Putin left his bilateral meeting with Trump on Thursday in “excellent spirits”, Russia’s state-run Tass news service said, citing Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov.

The trilateral has been called historic and unprecedented and “it really is”, Dennis Wilder, an ex-CIA official who is now a senior fellow at Georgetown University, told Bloomberg TV. “In terms of outcomes, the meeting really is the message.”

title: Honda debuts hybrid SUV for Asia in pivot from failed EV bet
article:
(Nov 20): Honda Motor Co unwrapped a new flagship SUV, the first of a range of gas-electric hybrid models the company is rolling out this decade as part of its pivot away from fully electric cars.

The Avancier will go on sale next spring, targeting markets including Japan, China and Australia, Honda said on Friday. The manufacturer declined to reveal the price of the 6-seater sport utility vehicle that will be built primarily in Thailand.

Honda is ramping up its hybrid offerings to take advantage of surging demand for the category around the world. The Japanese company plans to introduce 15 new gas-electric models by March 2030, primarily targeting North America.

The Avancier won’t make it to the US, Honda’s biggest sales market, the company said. It will instead occupy the highest rung of the brand’s SUV lineup in the Asia-Pacific region, placing it above the popular CR-V. It will be the first to use Honda’s new hybrid drivetrain that features a more powerful engine and more efficient electric motor.

“Our market share in large vehicles is lower than that of our competitors, and we’re looking to build a stronger foothold,” said Junichi Miyahara, a product planner for Honda.

Japanese carmakers and South Korea’s Hyundai Motor Co are benefiting from a rebound in demand for hybrids as EV growth remains uneven across the world. Toyota Motor Corp expects its gas-electric sales to exceed five million units for the first time this year. Honda is doubling down on hybrids after its ill-timed EV investments prompted a ¥2.5 trillion impairment charge and its first-ever annual loss.

See also: Japan’s CPI picks up, keeping BOJ on track for rate hike

In the key US market, Honda is planning a new US$3 billion factory in Ohio to make next-generation hybrids. It’s also preparing new gas-electric options for its large SUVs popular there, such as the Pilot and Acura MDX.

But Honda can’t completely abandon investments in EVs as they’re becoming increasingly important in Europe, Southeast Asia, India and especially China, said Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Tatsuo Yoshida. In the world’s biggest car market, Honda’s sales fell 53% in September.

“Neglecting battery EVs now could leave Honda exposed when market conditions shift again,” Yoshida said.

title: Xi embraces Trump as China’s best option to contain chip row
article:
(Nov 20): Chinese leader Xi Jinping showed US President Donald Trump extraordinary hospitality during their third summit of the year. For Beijing, that bonhomie might be its best strategy for stopping a spiralling chip battle with its main rival.

China’s top leader broke nearly five decades of precedent to give Trump a rare airport welcome — and cheek-to-cheek hug — as the Republican touched down on Wednesday in Shenzhen. Over an afternoon of discussions at a secluded state guesthouse the following day, Trump lauded Xi as a friend, while Xi praised his US counterpart’s effort to steady bilateral ties as “one for the history books”.

In another show of closeness, Trump, 80, was seen offering Xi, 73, a hand as they boarded an escalator, with the Chinese leader holding the Republican’s forearm as he stepped up beside him.

The camaraderie stood out coming days after Washington stepped up efforts to restrict China’s access to the technology underpinning the global artificial intelligence (AI) race. Both leaders appeared to lean heavily on their personal rapport to keep ties between the world’s largest economies on an even keel, a departure from the tit-for-tat of last year’s trade war.

“Trump is Xi’s best option,” said Alicia Garcia Herrero, the chief Asia-Pacific economist of Natixis SA. Officials in Beijing realise newly exposed divisions within the administration are driving the latest curbs, giving Beijing an incentive to preserve its relationship with the president. “Things could get worse. China needs to stop this spiral of additional export controls. It’s very important for China.”

Xi’s team now needs to “negotiate night and day” with the friendly pockets of Trump’s team before next month’s Group of 20 leaders’ summit in Miami, she said, and hold off on reimposing controls on rare earths — a move that would blow up their hard-won trade truce.

See also: US proposes curbs on investment in Chinese biotech firms

China’s resolve will be tested later this month when its suspension of a ban on exports of critical minerals to the US, including gallium, germanium and antimony, is set to expire. In a sign Beijing is already mulling some retaliation, China’s Commerce Ministry earlier this week threatened countermeasures against Washington’s latest salvo, if some resolution couldn’t be reached.

For now, this week’s summitry offered evidence that both leaders remain determined to prevent their rivalry from spiraling into a confrontation that would inflict pain on their own economies.

“You are my friend, and we have a very special relationship,” Trump told Xi at the start of their meeting, while flanked by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, whose agencies helped draft the latest curbs. “I think as long as you and I are in charge of things, we’ll never have a problem,” added the US president, who has two years left in the White House.

See also: US, China release product lists for US$30 bil tariff deal

After the Xi-Trump huddle spilled over into an impromptu lunch that kept Russian President Vladimir Putin waiting for their delayed trilateral, China called the discussions “positive and constructive”. Both sides vowed to develop an action plan for building a “constructive relationship of strategic stability”, and pledged greater cooperation on AI and drug controls, according to the Chinese readout.

“Any disagreements that cannot be resolved immediately should be managed constructively to prevent conflicts from escalating,” Xi said, in a veiled reference to Washington’s latest barrage of measures.

The US has yet to publish its own account of the talks.

Zhu Feng, the dean of the School of International Studies at Nanjing University, called the encounter on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum the “friendliest, most positive” meeting between Xi and Trump this year. The aftermath from Nvidia Corp co-founder Jensen Huang’s downfall, however, could still spark a major escalation in the US-China tech war, and change the calculus, he said.

“It is clear this summit will not alter the fundamental choices the US has made to engage in strategic competition with China,” he said. “China-US relations are unlikely to undergo any substantive change as a result of summit-level diplomacy. We need not harbor excessive illusions in this regard.”

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

The talks on Thursday were held in Kylin Villa, which opened in 1997, the year neighbouring Hong Kong was handed back to Beijing from Britain. That resort has since hosted Chinese leaders and high-profile foreign visitors, and is also personal to Xi being the place where his father — Xi Zhongxun — once recuperated while battling cancer.

Its lakeside location contrasts sharply with the rest of futuristic Shenzhen: the beating heart of China’s robotics and drone industries and home to Huawei Technologies Co — the national champion chasing Nvidia to produce cutting-edge AI chips.

China’s decision to host its summit in that city ensured the tech battle with America was the backdrop to the pleasantries, as the next deadline for extending their trade truce on Jan 10 looms large.

Trump tried to reduce tensions by downplaying allegations Huang had an affair with a Chinese executive who US intelligence believes was spying for China. “Any pretty woman that comes from China, they considered her to be a spy,” he said.

The US leader also appeared keen to distinguish between restricting China’s access to the most sophisticated semiconductors and allowing US companies to continue selling less advanced products.

Expectations for major breakthroughs were low going into the summit, especially given both leaders are meeting again next month. But even a commencement date for the reduction on US$30 billion ($38.7 billion) worth of each other’s imports, negotiated under the newly established US-China Board of Trade, didn’t materialise in the initial readouts. A similar framework has been floated for bilateral investment, though progress has been slow.

Tensions could soon flare again. US lawmakers in Washington are closing in on a deal to ban Chinese cars from the US, according to people familiar with the matter.

For now, both presidents want to reinforce their personal ties ahead of a potentially more confrontational period when the new US Congress takes office in January, said William Yang, a senior analyst for Northeast Asia at the International Crisis Group.

“The Democrats are signalling strongly they are going to look hard into pushing the administration to enforce or reinstate strict export control measures against high-end AI semiconductor chips,” he said. “Beijing is sensing there might be a storm coming in the next few weeks.”

title: Japan’s CPI picks up, keeping BOJ on track for rate hike
article:
(Nov 20): Gains by Japan’s consumer prices inched up to the fastest pace this year, firming up the case for the Bank of Japan (BOJ) to raise its benchmark interest rate next month.

The consumer price index excluding fresh food picked up for a second month to 2.2% in October compared with a year earlier, the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications reported on Friday. While it was the biggest advance since December, the result was a tad weaker than the median economist forecast of 2.3%.

The index that strips out both fresh food and energy, a measure closely monitored by the BOJ as a measure of underlying inflation, also climbed 2.2%, and overall CPI rose 2.3%.

Energy costs drove gains in the latest month, with overall energy prices rising 2.2% on year, reversing from a decline in September. The increase in costs related to mobile phones accelerated to 17.2% from 10.9%, also pushing the overall index higher.

“This was weaker than expected as various temporary factors at play including government measures and a plunge in rice prices,” said Masato Koike, senior economist at Sompo Institute Plus. “Japan’s inflation is likely to accelerate further towards 3% mainly due to the impact of the Middle East conflict, and the BOJ will probably stay vigilant against upside price risks.”

See also: Japan's central bank chief unfazed by consumption drop, stays open to rate hike

Friday’s data will bolster the case for raising the benchmark interest rate when the BOJ’s board meets in December. The bank has made it clear that its policy aim is no longer to coax underlying inflation higher towards its 2% target but rather to anchor it around that level. Last month it said underlying inflation reached the target for the first time since the goal was established in 2013.

As of Friday morning in Tokyo, swap contracts implied a roughly 86% probability that the bank will raise its policy rate on Dec 18. Koike said he’s among those expecting a move next month.

Service prices — a key measure of the sustainability of inflation — increased 1.4% from a year earlier. Gains in food prices excluding fresh items slowed to 2.2%, as rice prices dropped almost 30% the biggest decline in the data going back to 1971. A year ago, rice was among major drivers of overall inflation.

See also: Japan's Rakuten Bank shares tank as securities arm faces data breach

As has been the case for some time, the latest inflation report was distorted somewhat by government fiscal steps aimed at reining in utility costs. Those measures shaved almost one percentage point from overall CPI, the ministry said.

The elevated inflation is likely to reinforce Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s resolve to cut the sales tax on food for two years from April, especially after the US midterm election underscored how important it is for political leaders to address in soaring living costs.

Japan’s core inflation rate has exceeded the BOJ’s 2% target for the last four fiscal years through March 2026. The BOJ’s latest forecasts — that don’t factor in the impact of the consumption tax cut — suggest that trend will continue for two more years.

The BOJ’s economic projections last month pointed to further increases in the cost of living. Its price forecast of 2.5% growth for the current fiscal year would require core inflation to advance at a pace exceeding 3% as a monthly average until March, given data to date.

Businesses have been nimble in responding to the operational burden stemming from heightened costs for everything from energy to shipping and packaging, a result of the Iran war along with persistent yen weakness. Also, a labour crunch has forced companies to raise wages to retain staff. Japan’s major food and beverage companies are planning to raise the price of 1,477 items this month, almost ten times more than a year ago, according to Teikoku Databank.

Most of the upward pressure on prices is coming from external forces, according to Koike.

“Consumer spending is weak and not generating strong homemade inflationary pressures, so businesses are watching both the weakness and price pressures coming from the Middle East situation,” he said.

title: Dollar heads for fourth week of gains following Anthropic IPO
article:
(Nov 20): The dollar is headed for a fourth straight weekly gain as demand tied to the Anthropic PBC IPO further lifts the currency that has been supported by expectations of further Federal Reserve interest-rate hikes and elevated US Treasury yields.

The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index is up 0.7% this week — on track for its longest winning weekly streak since Oct 9. The advance comes as artificial intelligence lab Anthropic shares began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on Thursday. The biggest-ever public debut created more demand for the dollar as investors across the globe converted their currency to buy shares in the company. Anthropic stock jumped 17% on its first day of trading.

“A fair estimate of foreign take-up of the IPO is probably in the US$10 billion to US$15 billion range,” Brent Donnelly, president of Spectra Markets, wrote in a note on Thursday. “Those US dollar buyers are racing against corporates who are trying to get their US dollar buying done before Thanksgiving.”

While Anthropic is seen as a bellwether for the future of AI, the boom in the technology has already influenced Wall Street’s long-term dollar forecasts. Barclays Plc, Deutsche Bank AG and Standard Chartered Bank expect the dollar to extend its rally into 2027, citing US dominance in AI and its potential to lift productivity and interest rates. Anthropic’s listing adds to the appeal of the US equity market and positions the company to become one of the world’s most important stocks in the space.

See also: China sets strongest yuan fixing since 2022 as Apec begins

Foreign inflows into US stocks jumped 43% to US$670 billion in the January-September period, the highest since at least 2016, according to data from the Department of the Treasury compiled by Bloomberg.

The dollar gauge is up more than 3% this year, strengthening against most of its major peers.

Nomura strategist Dominic Bunning said the world’s reserve currency is benefiting from other sources of support this week. Treasury yields near recent highs are keeping carry trades in the dollar’s favour, Bunning added. The US 10-year yield is poised for its longest stretch above 5% since 2007.

See also: Indonesian rupiah falls to record low as Fed bets boost dollar

Meanwhile, Wednesday’s Fed minutes from its latest meeting showed nearly all officials agreed the central bank would likely need to raise rates “in the months ahead” to return inflation to their 2% target in a timely manner. And concerns that violence in the Middle East could escalate added to inflation worries and lifted oil prices.

“This week’s been all about de-risking,” said Alex Cohen, a strategist at Bank of America Corp. “US data and Fed speakers have delivered a message that further rate hikes are coming and justified. That’s a good mix for the US dollar.”

title: Oil set for third weekly drop as ample supply outweighs war risk
article:
(Nov 20): Oil edged higher on Friday after a volatile session on Thursday, with futures on track for a third weekly decline as traders weigh the risk of renewed US strikes on Iran against ample supply.

Brent traded above US$92 a barrel after swinging in a range of more than US$2 in the previous session, and is down almost 4% this week. The most-active contract for West Texas Intermediate (WTI) traded near US$83.

US President Donald Trump told Axios he was “not rushing into any decision” on Iran, while Energy Secretary Chris Wright on Fox News played down concerns about regional supplies, saying flows through the Strait of Hormuz have reached a record. The comments tempered concerns after Western officials said that the chances of the US launching another round of strikes against Iran had risen in recent days.

Global benchmark Brent has retreated by about a fifth this month, as supplies from the Middle East recovered and Trump held off on renewed strikes. Still, there has been a flare-up in low-level fighting across the region in recent days, including a spate of attacks on vessels transiting the critical Strait of Hormuz, and strikes by Tehran-backed Houthis on Riyadh.

“While the near-term rise in geopolitical tensions is bringing some buying back to crude, the overall fundamentals are still moving more bearish,” said Dennis Kissler, a senior vice-president for trading at BOK Financial Securities Inc, pointing to Iraq selling physical crude at steep discounts.

The International Energy Agency forecasts a roughly two-million barrel-a-day surplus this quarter, underscoring the increasing bearish supply backdrop. Goldman Sachs Group Inc has flagged the risk of a glut next year.

See also: Vietnam triples LNG imports as El Niño saps hydropower output

Elsewhere, the leaders of the US, China and Russia agreed to “increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations” at a meeting in Shenzhen on Thursday, according to a joint statement. They didn’t spell out what that would entail.

title: Asian stocks fall as Anthropic slips in after-hours
article:
(Nov 20): Asian stocks sold off on Friday as pessimism over the artificial-intelligence (AI) trade hammered technology shares, with global equities set for their longest losing streak in three years. Anthropic PBC fell in after-hours trading.

MSCI Inc’s Asia-Pacific equities index fell 1.7% — extending its decline to a seventh straight session — and poised for its lowest close since April. That pushed the MSCI All Country World Index — a key barometer of global stocks — on course for its longest losing streak since September 2023.

Anthropic, the maker of Claude, declined over 5% after hours to below US$92 ($119), slipping beneath its lowest level during Thursday’s stock-market debut. The shares had closed 17% above their IPO price even after Apple Inc said it’s developing its own AI agent to rival OpenAI and Anthropic.

“Investors are questioning whether frontier AI is becoming a hugely successful technology but an increasingly difficult business in which to earn attractive returns,” said Charu Chanana, the chief investment strategist of Saxo Markets. “Apple’s reported move to develop its own AI agent only reinforces these concerns.”

Investors have retreated from one of the hottest corners of the market this year as mounting doubts over the AI trade pressure technology stocks. At the heart of the concern is whether returns from the boom will ultimately justify the vast sums being spent and borrowed to fund it, fuelling a broader decline in global equities.

See also: Stocks fluctuate after Anthropic IPO, copper gains

“The Anthropic IPO has been a major success,” said Matt Maley at Miller Tabak. “However, the IPO does little to address the market’s bigger problems including AI profitability concerns, massive spending, higher interest rates, credit market stress and geopolitical risks.”

Elsewhere, emerging-market currencies slumped in US hours as a gauge of dollar strength hovered near its highest level since April 2025, the Bloomberg Commodity Index sank to its lowest since July and Treasuries rallied as investors sought haven assets.

Sentiment remained weak as futures for the S&P 500 Index dropped 0.3%, pointing to further losses for the US benchmark, which posted its longest slide since 2024. Contracts for the Nasdaq 100 Index fell 0.6%, after the underlying gauge closed at its lowest level since April.

See also: Global stocks, US futures rebound after Nvidia earnings

“The initial euphoria around Anthropic’s listing is starting to fade a little, and that strong first-day performance isn’t translating into broader enthusiasm across the AI sector,” said Tim Waterer, the chief market analyst at KCM Trade.

Beyond technology, oil prices swung amid concern that violence in the Middle East will re-escalate despite pressure on US President Donald Trump to pursue a diplomatic resolution to the nine-month war.

The most-active contract for West Texas Intermediate traded near US$83 a barrel, after swinging in a range of more than US$2 in the previous session, and is down 5% for the week. Brent settled near US$92.

Gold fell and was heading for the biggest weekly decline since March, as hawkish Federal Reserve (Fed) officials signalled more interest-rate hikes and a sell-off in AI stocks pushed investors to sell the metal to cover losses.

Bullion dropped as much as 1% on Friday to near US$3,590 an ounce, on track to lose more than 7% in a week that’s seen the metal slide to the lowest since September 2025. Silver has lost around 13% in the same period.

Meanwhile, Treasuries rallied, pushing yields lower across maturities, though the move offered only a reprieve from the broader pressure on the bond market. The 10-year yield, at around 5.02%, is poised to match its 2007 run of 29 closes above 5% in a single year.

A stream of comments from Fed officials in recent days has reinforced expectations for further tightening. Traders expect the central bank to hike in December, followed by two more increases in 2027.

Chicago Fed president Austan Goolsbee said he will consider all options when policymakers meet next month and didn’t push back against the possibility of a larger-than-usual rate increase.

“We have now had multiple months in a row of borderline disturbingly high inflation rates with little progress in the sectors where we would expect to be seeing some progress,” Goolsbee told reporters on Thursday. “So everything’s always on the table, in my view, and how steep that path needs to be is determined by what we think is happening with inflation.”
