title: JPMorgan, Visa, Mastercard warn of cyberattack that hit outside vendor
article:
(Nov 20): JPMorgan Chase & Co, Visa Inc and Mastercard Inc said some customer information was accessed in a cyberattack on a vendor.

JPMorgan said it believes, based on an investigation so far, that hackers accessed marketing data held by an outside firm, which may include customer names and email addresses. The bank said the issue isn’t related to an outage it faced earlier this week.

The bank said there’s no disruption to its services and that it will contact customers who were affected and offer support, such as credit monitoring services, according to a statement on Thursday.

Visa said it was an incident tied to a third-party company in Asia and the payments firms’ own systems weren’t involved. Payments data, such as card numbers, weren’t affected, the firm said. Mastercard also said that the data exposed was a “limited amount of non-payments information from a subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit programme” and that it appeared to be mostly email addresses. The company that there wasn’t any impact to its network.

Visa shares were down 2.9% to US$403.24 ($520.75) at 11.14am in New York on Thursday. Mastercard shares fell 2.1% while JPMorgan shares were down about 0.9%.

A string of digital issues in recent weeks have spurred fears about the safety of technology powering some of the biggest companies. Earlier this week, JPMorgan faced an outage that affected customers, a disruption that the firm has said wasn’t related to cybersecurity.

See also: MAS warns AI agents could move money faster, raise finance risks

Trump administration officials have said that Iranian cyberattacks have targeted US critical infrastructure and networks since the war began earlier this year, but stressed that many recent outages were unrelated.

Some executives have warned that there could be more disruptions ahead. Earlier this year, the release of new artificial intelligence models that are better at spotting necessary fixes in companies’ cybersecurity armour spurred companies to work on tightening controls.

But the high volume of fixes needed is likely to result in more disruptions, according to Citigroup Inc chief executive officer Jane Fraser.

title: Apple working on AI agent for device control, apps, browsing and coding
article:
(Nov 20): Apple Inc is developing its own autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) agent that can get things done on behalf of users, looking to enter a fast-growing market already being pursued by OpenAI, Anthropic PBC, Meta Platforms Inc and others.

The company outlined the plans in job listings added to its website this week. In one, Apple said it’s seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant. The system will write code, browse the web, control apps and navigate devices on a user’s behalf, according to the post.

The move follows the breakout success of Meta’s Muse, which has captured the attention of consumers in recent months with its ability to make restaurant reservations, book travel and prepare news briefings. There’s also been a proliferation of tools that let AI control Mac computers and programme software.

Shares of Meta and Anthropic slid in late trading after Bloomberg News reported on Apple’s efforts. Meta fell nearly 2%, while Anthropic dropped more than 3%.

Anthropic PBC recently widened user testing of its own agent, called Duet, while OpenAI has expanded the capabilities of Dots. And Alphabet Inc’s Google overhauled its agent, now called Tasks, earlier this week. Like Elon Musk’s Grok Bot, Tasks lets the system make phone calls on a user’s behalf — in addition to offering standard AI agent features.

Apple’s App Store has been dominated by AI agents, with Muse long occupying the No 2 spot among free apps, just behind TikTok, on Thursday. OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude were also both in the top five.

See also: Anthropic shares jump 17% after US$107.3 bil IPO breaks record

OpenAI, Anthropic and Musk’s SpaceXSI are also behind popular developer coding tools Codex, Claude Code and Cursor.

Bloomberg News reported earlier this month that Apple was developing its own AI agent offering, but the new job listings offer fresh evidence of the company’s plans. Apple has eyed introducing the service as soon as the end of next year, but development remains in the early stages. An Apple spokesperson didn’t respond to a request for comments.

“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” the job listing reads. “It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple.”

See also: Nvidia boosts forecast while quashing idea of Huang’s return

The listing says the company has a team building the “foundation for that future” and that Apple is looking for the hired manager to “make it real”. John Ternus, the tech giant’s new chief executive officer, has been pushing software engineering chief Craig Federighi to move faster and take a bolder approach to AI — with an agent being key to that effort.

“People already do their most valuable work by moving fluidly between tools: a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, a service. We are building AI agents that can do the same,” the listing says. The posting adds that Apple is working on agents that can “plan and carry out multistep tasks” across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and application programming interfaces, and they can “coordinate specialised subagents along the way”.

The company strongly indicates its platform would be capable of autonomously navigating the interfaces of its operating systems. The listing specifically mentions development of “general-purpose computer-use agents”, the technology that allows ChatGPT and Muse to control a Mac. Google Gemini added such functionality earlier on Thursday.

Another central component is privacy, with Apple saying that safety needs to be built into the system’s design. “Agents that can run code, use credentials, and act on a user’s behalf need strong permission models, sandboxing and transparency.”

Sandboxing refers to a process that lets engineers test software without the risk of it breaking out into external networks, the rest of the operating system or the broader internet.

As the company develops its own agent, Apple is also making it more difficult for competing bots to gain broad control over its computers. In the beta version of the forthcoming macOS 27.3 operating system, the company has introduced new warning screens that prompt users to reconsider granting third-party agents permission to control their Macs.

With the change in 27.3, ChatGPT users now need to engage in 14 distinct steps to enable support for third-party computer-use tools, up from four. While Apple has positioned the shift as a move to protect customers, some AI companies and users see it as an attempt to slow down the competition.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Apple has already been sued by the US Justice Department for actions such as blocking third-party access to features and hardware.

While Apple is still far from introducing its own full-fledged AI agent, it has taken steps to integrate its Siri digital assistant more deeply into third-party apps. The company’s upcoming iOS 27.3 release lays the groundwork for deeper collaboration between Siri AI and outside applications, allowing the assistant to, say, book a car or restaurant reservation.

Still, the updated system doesn’t go as far as a fully fledged agent, which can autonomously carry out complex tasks across multiple apps and services in the background with little additional instruction from the user.

title: Anthropic shares jump 17% after US$107.3 bil IPO breaks record
article:
(Nov 20): Anthropic PBC shares soared 17% above their initial public offering (IPO) price in the biggest offering on record, raising US$107.3 billion ($138.6 billion) despite signs of growing caution around the artificial intelligence (AI) trade.

Shares of the AI lab closed at US$97.17 on Thursday in New York, paring an opening surge that took it far above the IPO price of US$83. That gives Anthropic a fully diluted market value of about US$1.8 trillion, making it one of the 10 biggest public companies in the world by market cap.

The deal follows weeks of shaky trading in US stocks, as investors grapple with factors ranging from worries over Nvidia Corp’s role as a major backstop of the AI ecosystem following its long-time chief’s ouster to a Democratic sweep in midterm elections that promises to change the industry’s regulatory landscape. Some of that nervousness was reflected in broader markets on Thursday, with the S&P 500 Index falling 2% and the Nasdaq 100 Index off 2.2%.

“You have seen sentiment sort of continue to worsen around AI and it has not let up today,” said Jordan Watson, the managing director of investments at Tandem Investment Advisors. “What’s important for markets now is Anthropic is the most transparent real-time signal of the AI risk trade.”

Anthropic’s long-awaited debut marks the first ever by a frontier AI lab, a cohort of firms building the most advanced models to tackle difficult problems and assist users in complex tasks. While enthusiasm over AI’s business potential has spurred massive investments in infrastructure such as chips and data centres, Anthropic and its competitors now need to grow revenue fast enough to outpace those ambitious spending plans.

The company behind the Claude chatbot and its seven co-founders raised US$81.3 billion in an IPO priced above range, topping SpaceX’s IPO in June, and another US$26 billion in a concurrent private placement. The debut puts Anthropic firmly ahead of rival OpenAI, which is not planning to go public before 2027.

See also: Nvidia boosts forecast while quashing idea of Huang’s return

Overall demand for the IPO neared seven times the number of shares available, Bloomberg News reported on Sunday, with two more days of formal marketing before the company stopped taking orders.

The line-up of investors in Anthropic’s private placement is a who’s who of the AI trade, including Nvidia Corp, Alphabet Inc’s Google, Microsoft Corp and Advanced Micro Devices Inc, according to its filings, a reflection of the tight relationships within the sector.

See also: Nvidia stops selling AI chips to China despite US approval

At the same time, Anthropic’s IPO left more than half of the institutional investors bidding for stock without any shares, people familiar with the matter have said.

Meanwhile, retail investors received about 15% of the shares available, according to people familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified as the information isn’t public. A representative of Anthropic declined to comment. The Wall Street Journal reported the level earlier.

The company counts Nvidia as a strategic partner, and has committed tens of billions of dollars to deals securing access to its most advanced chips. Discussions about so-called circular financing and whether firms backing their heaviest users may be inflating a bubble have intensified as tech stocks have churned in recent weeks.

The exit of Nvidia’s long-time chief executive officer Jensen Huang earlier this month further magnified those worries, adding to investor unease following a resounding Democratic victory in midterm elections that bolstered momentum for more AI safety regulation and could lead to tighter state-level restrictions on data centre construction.

Thursday’s broader market weakness was “just a continuation of what we have seen for the last several weeks, and that is a lot of nervousness around the semiconductor space”, said Gina Martin Adams, the chief market strategist of HB Wealth. “The financing of the AI ecosystem is certainly a question that investors are asking and it’s weighing on the market at large.”

Some of the broader sell-off may have also been fuelled by investors selling positions in other companies to buy Anthropic shares, she added.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Anthropic’s origin story centres around former OpenAI executives defecting because they wanted to prioritise AI safety. Nearly six years after its founding, Anthropic has structured itself as a public benefit corporation that balances shareholder interests with those of society, and whose governance includes a long-term benefit trust that has the power to elect and remove a majority of the members of the company’s board.

Regulators, investors and even Anthropic’s employees have flagged the significant risk of humans losing control of the technology, with one putting the chance of AI eliminating all humans in the next decade at greater than 10%. Bill Gates said AI is powerful enough to drive events that cause “a billion deaths”.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is among those calling for top AI labs to “pace the frontier” in order to prioritise safety. Still, a focus on caution hasn’t stopped the company from turning into a juggernaut, with revenue projections well above many large companies that have been around for decades.

The company won over investors with a focus on enterprise customers, propelling its run-rate revenue — a measure annualised from a shorter period — to US$81 billion as of Oct 31, up US$10 billion from the end of September, its regulatory filings showed.

Claude Code, the company’s coding agent for software developers, is widely adopted in the industry and has even been used by Nasa engineers, the filing showed. Anthropic has more than 11,900 customers delivering US$100,000 of revenue each on a trailing 12-month basis as of the end of September, up from about 1,500 in 2025.

The company aims to expand its footprint in more professions from law to healthcare. Anthropic counts Novartis AG CEO Vas Narasimhan as one of its board members.

A major challenge will be taming ballooning costs for AI infrastructure and reliably delivering operational profitability. Anthropic reported a US$567 million operating loss in the third quarter, primarily driven by US$5 billion of computing costs under short-term commitments and US$2 billion of non-cash charges related to the company’s charitable donation-matching programme.

Goldman Sachs Group Inc research analysts expect the company to take until 2030 to generate positive free cash flow on an annual basis, Bloomberg News reported. That said, they are modelling for Anthropic’s annual revenue to soar to roughly US$685 billion by 2030, Bloomberg News has reported. To pull off that feat, it will need to fend off AI pricing pressures from cheaper open-weight models, including from Chinese developers.

Anthropic’s listing joins companies linked to AI that have pushed US IPO volume to an all-time high. Including Anthropic, first time stock sales raised nearly US$246 billion this year through Wednesday, beating 2021’s $195 billion haul, excluding financial vehicles such as blank-cheque firms, data compiled by Bloomberg showed.

This year’s total was bolstered by SpaceX’s debut, which leaned heavily on its market opportunity in AI for its IPO pitch to investors, and South Korean memory chipmaker SK Hynix Inc’s US$26.5 billion American depositary receipt sale.

In addition to the 980 million shares sold in the IPO, as many as 315 million shares can be offered on the first day of trading by non-founder employees, board members and former staffers, including chief financial officer Krishna Rao, Anthropic’s filings showed. About 15.5 billion shares held by insiders are subject to lock-up agreements that extend until after it reports results in the third quarter of next year.

Anthropic is expected to see a lift from index-tracking funds generating billions of dollars in demand. If it qualifies for early inclusion, it could join the Russell 1000 and the Nasdaq 100 as soon as December. FTSE Russell and Nasdaq changed their rules this year to speed the inclusion of large new listings.

Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley led Anthropic’s IPO, with participation from 20 other banks, the filings showed. The stock trades on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT.

title: Stocks fall as Anthropic debut not an AI all-clear
article:
(Nov 20) : A rally in stocks fizzled out as Anthropic PBC’s solid market debut failed to sustain enthusiasm for the artificial-intelligence trade.

The sharp reversal drove the S&P 500 down 2%, with the gauge posting its longest slide since April 2024. Shares of the AI lab pared their surge to trade 17% above the IPO price. Advanced Micro Devices Inc. sank on a Hunterbrook Capital short-call that cited China risks. AMD denied any wrongdoing.

Wall Street’s fresh bout of volatility engulfed the broader market, with more than 460 firms in the US equity benchmark retreating. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed on the verge of a technical correction. All megacaps fell.

While Anthropic’s debut was a historic moment for AI, it also took place during an unsettling moment for the industry. Tech stocks have been under pressure as investors question whether the AI boom will ultimately generate returns large enough to justify the industry’s borrowing binge.

“The Anthropic IPO has been a major success,” said Matt Maley at Miller Tabak. “However, the IPO does little to address the market’s bigger problems including AI profitability concerns, massive spending, higher interest rates, credit market stress and geopolitical risks.”

The stock began trading Thursday on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT.

See also: Stocks fall on Nvidia rout as Anthropic in focus

Anthropic’s IPO is a huge win for the AI trade because it proves investors aren’t running away, which was one of the fears driving the spending slowdown thesis, according to Luke Lango, editor of the Innovation Investor newsletter.

“But don’t mistake one blockbuster deal for an all-clear signal,” he said. “Wall Street writing a check to the world’s leading frontier lab, a company with explosive revenue growth and customers lining up for more, is very different from Wall Street writing checks to debt-heavy neoclouds and the riskier corners of the AI stack.”

The first is a bet on the winner, said Lango. The second is a bet on the buildout, and that’s where money has gotten a lot pickier, he added.

See also: Stocks fall on tech disruptions as Nvidia in focus

With hundreds of billions of dollars committed to infrastructure such as chips and data centers, the next challenge for the top AI labs is to grow revenue fast enough to outpace the industry’s ambitious spending plans.

“Anthropic will need to show that it can expand the use of its models while containing the cost of meeting that demand,” said Antonio Di Giacomo at XS.com.
